matched_findings.found_description: The `_updateCurrent()` function is only called by `update()`, which is guarded by `onlyFactory`. However, `_updateCurrent()` internally calls `oracles[++global.current] = Epoch(newProvider, uint96(newProvider.current()))`, which sets the timestamp of the new oracle to `newProvider.current()`. The `current()` function returns a raw price value (e.g., 1.5e18 for $1.50). If an attacker gains access to the factory (e.g., via compromised admin or governance), they can call `update()` with a malicious provider that returns a manipulated `current()` value (e.g., 0). This sets the new oracle's timestamp to 0, which is then used in `_handleLatest()` and `at()` to determine the latest valid version. If the attacker then calls `request()` with a timestamp just after the last valid one, the system may accept the 0-timestamped oracle as the latest, causing all subsequent price queries to return 0. This allows the attacker to trigger liquidations at 0 price (stealing collateral) or prevent settlements. The economic impact: users lose collateral to liquidators, and the protocol becomes insolvent. The access control is technically present, but the state update function `_updateCurrent()` allows arbitrary timestamp injection via `current()`, which is not validated for reasonableness.

market funds by utilizing the adiabatic fees change. The adiabatic fees are fees
taken from takers when they increase skew (difference between open longs and
shorts) and paid to takers when they decrease skew to incentivize orders which
reduce price risk for makers. The issue is that market coordinator can set adiabatic
fees to 0, open large maker/taker positions (taker position paying 0 adiabatic fees),
then immediately set adiabatic fees to max possible (e.g. 1%) and close
taker/maker positions (receiving the adiabatic fee). This fees difference when
adiabatic fees are changed by market coordinator is subtracted from market 's
globalexposure , which is supposed to be paid/received by the owner. I.e. when
adiabatic fees are increased, this increases exposure to be paid by the owner with
coordinator being able to withdraw this amount to himself (up to total market 's
collateral available), meaning coordinator can steal all market funds.

pinpoint any specific code which is the root cause.

to control the owner 's exposure, which is essentially what lets coordinator to take
advantage of this and steal funds.
Internal pre-conditions Coordinator is malicious OR User front-runs adiabatic fees
increase transaction
External pre-conditions None.
Attack Path
1. Coordinator sets adiabatic fees and all the other fees to 0, also increases
maker Limit to large amount to cause larger impact
2. Coordinator opens large maker position and large taker position (paying 0
fees)
3. Wait for 1 oracle version to settle maker and taker positions
4. Coordinator sets adiabatic fees to max allowed value (e.g. 1%)
5. Coordinator closes taker position, settles it, closes maker position, settles it

deposited, and taker should have deposited collateral + adiabatic fees paid to
taker for closing the position. Both maker and taker accounts withdraw all
collateral. Most likely total collateral will be higher than the market has, so
simply withdraw all collateral market has

maybe maker position if necessary, to be able to open large taker positions).
This doesn 't need to be classic front-run, maybe the coordinator will
announce risk parameter changes in the forum or somewhere, and user opens
these positions in anticipation of adiabatic fees increase
3. Coordinator transaction to increase adiabatic fees goes through
4. User closes his positions, receiving large profit from adiabatic fees only
(which should more than cover all the other fees, and market price risk can be
neutralized by opening delta-neutral positions), at the expense of the owner 's
exposure

Market coordinator can set both maker Limit andscale fortaker Fee at very low
amount (like 1), which will charge absurdly high taker proportional fee to existing
positions, because proportional fee formula is
change.abs ().mul (price).muldiv (change.abs (), scale).mul (fee) , i.e. the fee is
(order_size) ˆ2 * price * fee when scale is 1. The same issue is with maker
proportional fee and taker adiabatic fee - all of them multiply by order size divided
byscale .
The only limitation for scale setting is that it must be larger than some percentage
ofmaker Limit and there is no limitation on maker Limit :
UFixed 6 scale Limit =
self.maker Limit.div (self.efficiency Limit).mul (protocol Parameter.min Scale); ,!
if (self.taker Fee.scale.lt (scale Limit) || self.maker Fee.scale.lt (scale Limit))
revert Risk Parameter Storage Invalid Error ();
This allows to set any scale amount, the maker Limit just has to be set to a similar
amount, or alternatively efficiency Limit can be set to a huge amount (there is only
downside limitation for it), which will make scale Limit very low, allowing very low
scale values.
Market coordinator can abuse this by opening large maker position (settling it),
opening large taker position (unsettled), changing risk parameter maker Limit and
scale to 1, then at the next oracle version the large taker position will be settled
usingscale = 1 , charging fees much higher than 100%, putting taker position into
huge bad debt, while all makers will have huge profit (larger than market collateral),
11

which coordinator can immediately withdraw from his maker position, stealing all
market collateral.
Root Cause The exact root cause is hard to determine here. It might be the lack of
risk parameter settings validations: the only scale check is against scale Limit
calculated from maker Limit , but there is no conditions on maker Limit itself:
https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-08-perennial-v 2-update-3/blob/main/pere
nnial-v 2/packages/perennial/contracts/types/Risk Parameter.sol#L 159-L 161
On the other hand, it 's probably hard to set correct protocol-wide limitation for this,
so maybe the issue is with the design of the proportional and adiabatic fees, where
theorder_size / scale multiplication is quite dangerous as it is unlimited.
Internal pre-conditions Coordinator is malicious.
External pre-conditions None.
Attack Path
1. Coordinator opens large maker position, settles it
2. Coordinator opens large taker position (but doesn 't settle it yet)
3. Coordinator sets risk parameter: maker Limit = 1 , taker Fee.scale = 1 and
taker Fee.propotional Fee set to max.
4. Coordinator commits oracle version of the taker position, settles maker+taker
positions: taker is in huge bad debt, maker is in huge profit (larger than all
market collateral)
5. Coordinator withdraws all market collateral
Note: step 1 and 2 are preparation, steps 3-5 can be performed in 1 transaction
Alternatives:
•Settingtake Fee.scale = 1 andefficiency Limit to a very high value.
•All taker trades after the scale = 1 is set will incur huge fee, so it 's possible to
have settled taker position before the risk params change, and then close it by
liquidation, incuring huge fees. Coordinator doesn 't even have to open his own
taker position, he can simply liquidate any large existing taker.
•Use adiabatic fees scale instead of taker proportional fees
•Use maker propotional fees (and use only maker accounts)
Impact All market collateral stolen.
Additional impact: if the market is part of any vault, almost all this vault funds can
be stolen. This can be done by forcing the vault to re-balance (depositing or
withdrawing some amount), which will charge huge fees, making vault 's collateral in
12

the market negative. Next re-balance will add more collateral into the market,
which can be stolen again, repeated until most vault funds are stolen.

extra_findings.title: Incorrect Unit Handling in claimFee() Leads to Underpayment of Protocol Fees
extra_findings.description: The claimFee() function incorrectly handles the unit conversion when transferring protocol, oracle, and risk fees. It uses UFixed6Lib.ZERO and UFixed6 for fee accumulation, but then calls token.push(msg.sender, UFixed18Lib.from(feeReceived)) to transfer the fee. However, UFixed6 and UFixed18 have different decimal precisions (6 vs 18). The function accumulates fees in UFixed6 (1e-6 scale) but converts them to UFixed18 (1e-18 scale) using UFixed18Lib.from(), which does NOT perform a scaling conversion — it merely reinterprets the same numeric value as if it were in 18 decimals. This causes the fee to be underpaid by a factor of 1e12. For example, a protocol fee of 1.0 UFixed6 (1,000,000 in raw units) is interpreted as 1.0 UFixed18 (1 in raw units), resulting in a 99.9999% fee loss. This affects protocol, oracle, and risk fees, which are all subject to the same bug. The beneficiary and coordinator are systematically underpaid, leading to permanent loss of protocol revenue.

extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds Triggers Unauthorized Deposit Logic
extra_findings.description: The Market contract's _update function automatically transfers tokens to/from the sender when collateral changes occur, without verifying the source of the funds. This allows an attacker to send funds directly to the contract (e.g., via a withdrawal refund from an external system) and have those funds automatically processed as a deposit, effectively converting withdrawal returns into new deposits. This breaks the fundamental accounting separation between user-initiated deposits and system-generated returns, leading to incorrect position and collateral calculations.

extra_findings.title: Access Control Bypass on _processOrderGlobal and _processOrderLocal Enables Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The functions _processOrderGlobal and _processOrderLocal, which are responsible for settling positions and distributing fees (liquidation, solver, referrer fees), are called indirectly via _settle() without access control. Since _settle() is publicly callable by any user (via update() or settle()), an attacker can trigger settlement at arbitrary times to manipulate the timing of fee accrual and distribution. This allows the attacker to front-run or delay settlement to capture fees intended for legitimate referrers or the protocol, effectively stealing fee revenue. The state variables _pendingOrder, _guarantee, _versions, and _checkpoints are read and updated during settlement, and their timing-dependent state is critical for correct fee calculation. Because these functions lack access control, users can manipulate the timing of settlement relative to oracle price updates and pending order readiness, leading to misallocation of fees.

extra_findings.title: Unit Mismatch in _credit() Causes Incorrect Fee Distribution Due to Fixed6 vs UFixed6 Inconsistency
extra_findings.description: The _credit() function credits claimable amounts using UFixed6 (unsigned 6-decimal fixed point), but the accumulationResponse.liquidationFee, subtractiveFee, and solverFee returned by CheckpointLib.accumulate() and VersionLib.accumulate() are of type Fixed6 (signed 6-decimal fixed point). When a negative fee (e.g., a rebate) is generated, Fixed6 can be negative, but UFixed6 cannot represent negative values. When _credit() receives a negative Fixed6 value from accumulationResponse, it is implicitly cast to UFixed6, causing underflow and wrapping to a large positive value. This results in the attacker being credited with a massive, unintended fee amount. The call chain is: _processOrderLocal → CheckpointLib.accumulate() → returns Fixed6 fee → _credit() → casts to UFixed6 → wraps → credits attacker. This leads to direct theft of protocol collateral.

extra_findings.title: Desynchronized Order ID Iteration in _settle() Causes Missed Fee Claims and Position Updates
extra_findings.description: In _settle(), the while loops for processing global and local pending orders use context.global.latestId and context.local.latestId as iteration bounds. However, these latestId values are not updated atomically with the pending order storage. An attacker can submit a series of orders with increasing IDs, then call _settle() multiple times. Between calls, the attacker can call update() to increment context.global.latestId and context.local.latestId, but the pending order storage (_pendingOrder, _pendingOrders) is not cleared. This causes the while loops to skip orders whose IDs are between the old and new latestId values. For example, if latestId = 5, and an attacker calls update() to set latestId = 7, then _settle() will only process order ID 6 (if ready), skipping ID 7 entirely. This results in missed fee distributions (liquidation, referrer, solver fees) and unprocessed position updates, leading to permanent loss of fee revenue and incorrect position accounting. The attack is repeatable and scalable.

extra_findings.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in VersionLib.accumulate with Negative Exposure
extra_findings.description: The VersionLib.accumulate function, called during settlement, processes oracle data without validating that the exposure value is non-negative before performing logarithmic or square root operations (implied by fixed-point math library usage). The Fixed6 type can represent negative values, and if the global exposure becomes negative during settlement, mathematical functions like ln() or sqrt() may be applied to invalid inputs, producing undefined or meaningless results without error. This leads to incorrect position valuations and potential fund misallocation.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before External Call in _updateAndStore
extra_findings.description: In _updateAndStore, state is committed via _storeContext before the token transfer logic in _update. If the token.transfer (via token.pull/push) reverts due to insufficient balance or external contract failure, the position and order state changes are already committed, but the collateral transfer fails. This leaves the market with an inconsistent state: the user's position is updated and fees are accrued, but collateral is not transferred, creating a liability that cannot be recovered.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Not Bound in update Intent Signature Verification
extra_findings.description: The verifier.verifyIntent() validates the signature of the intent but does not bind the executor (msg.sender) to the signed intent. An attacker can front-run a legitimate intent by submitting the same signed intent with a malicious msg.sender (e.g., a contract that drains funds). The signature is valid, the intent is processed, but the attacker's address is used as the counterparty, allowing them to claim the position and collateral without having signed the intent.

extra_findings.title: Incomplete State Restoration in _settle During Oracle Version Failure
extra_findings.description: During _processOrderGlobal and _processOrderLocal, if the oracle version is invalid (oracleVersion.valid == false), the order and guarantee are invalidated via newOrder.invalidate() and newGuarantee.invalidate(). However, the global and local positions (context.latestPositionGlobal and context.latestPositionLocal) are still updated via update(newOrder) even when invalidated. This means the position is advanced to a timestamp with no valid price, but the order is marked invalid — creating a state where the position reflects a price that cannot be trusted, and no mechanism exists to roll it back.

extra_findings.title: Precision Loss in Fixed6 to UFixed18 Conversion During Token Transfers
extra_findings.description: In _update, collateral transfers use UFixed18Lib.from(newOrder.collateral.abs()). Since newOrder.collateral is Fixed6 (6 fractional bits), and UFixed18Lib.from() assumes 18 fractional bits, the conversion truncates the lower 12 bits of precision. For example, a collateral of 1.000001 (Fixed6) becomes 1.000000000000000000 (UFixed18), losing 0.000001 units. Over many trades, this accumulates into significant unaccounted-for funds, effectively a stealth tax on users.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Unit Handling in claimFee Leads to Underpayment of Oracle Fees
extra_findings.description: The claimFee function incorrectly handles unit conversion between UFixed6 and UFixed18, causing oracle fees to be underpaid by a factor of 10^12. The function claims a fee from the market using market.claimFee(address(this)), which returns a value in UFixed18 (18 decimals), but then attempts to return a portion of it to msg.sender using UFixed18Lib.from(settlementFeeRequested), where settlementFeeRequested is UFixed6 (6 decimals). This conversion is invalid because UFixed18Lib.from(UFixed6) does not perform a decimal scaling conversion — it merely reinterprets the raw value as UFixed18, effectively multiplying the intended fee by 10^12. As a result, the oracle provider factory receives 10^12 times less than intended, while the beneficiary receives 10^12 times more than intended. This is a critical accounting error that systematically steals value from the keeper (oracle provider factory) and overpays the beneficiary.

extra_findings.title: Desynchronized Oracle Version Iteration in `at()` Function Leads to Missing Historical Data
extra_findings.description: The `at()` function iterates backward through the `oracles` mapping using a loop that breaks when it encounters a timestamp lower than the target. However, the iteration bound is based on `global.current - 1` and decrements down to 1, skipping index 0 entirely. This means historical oracle versions at index 0 are permanently inaccessible, even if they are the only valid version for a given timestamp. Since `global.current` starts at 0 after initialization and increments only on `update()`, any oracle version stored at index 0 (the initial provider) is never accessible via `at()`, violating the contract's stated purpose of providing historical oracle data. This creates a data integrity breach where users and downstream systems (e.g., liquidation engines, settlement protocols) cannot retrieve valid historical prices, leading to incorrect valuations and potential insolvency events.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Unit Representation in `claimFee()` Leads to Fee Underpayment and Loss of Incentive Tokens
extra_findings.description: The `claimFee()` function receives `settlementFeeRequested` as a UFixed6 (6 decimal places) and uses it to transfer tokens via `UFixed18Lib.from(settlementFeeRequested)`, which converts it to UFixed18 (18 decimals). However, `market.claimFee(address(this))` returns a fee in the market's native token representation, which is likely UFixed18 (standard for Perennial). The function then subtracts the converted settlement fee from the received fee and emits the difference. But the problem is: `claimFee()` does not validate that the returned `feeReceived` is in the same unit as the settlement fee. If `market.claimFee()` returns a value in UFixed6 (e.g., 1000000 for 1 token), but `UFixed18Lib.from(settlementFeeRequested)` converts 1 UFixed6 (1000000) to 1e18 UFixed18, then the subtraction `feeReceived.sub(settlementFeeRequested)` becomes 1e6 - 1e18 = negative underflow (reverts) or massive underpayment if no revert. This unit mismatch causes the keeper to receive either 0 or a fraction of the intended fee, while the beneficiary loses the remainder. The economic impact is permanent loss of incentive tokens to the keeper and misallocation of oracle fees.

extra_findings.title: Oracle Fee Claim Allows Unauthorized Fund Extraction via msg.sender Spoofing
extra_findings.description: The claimFee function allows any address to claim fees by impersonating a registered oracle provider, because it only verifies msg.sender against the current or latest oracle provider addresses without binding the call to a specific authorization context. An attacker can deploy a malicious contract that forwards calls with the same address as a registered oracle provider, enabling them to claim the full settlement fee and receive the difference as a refund, effectively stealing funds from the market's incentive pool.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before Operation Completion in _updateCurrent
extra_findings.description: The _updateCurrent function increments global.current and updates the oracle registry before verifying that the new provider's status is valid or that the update can be safely applied. This commits state (global.current) before ensuring the operation will succeed, leaving the oracle in an inconsistent state if the provider's latest() or current() calls revert or return invalid data.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Latest Version Handling in _handleLatest Causes Incorrect Oracle Readouts
extra_findings.description: The _handleLatest function conditionally re-queries the oracle at a timestamp using the at() function, but does not validate that the returned version is semantically consistent with the provider's state. This can cause the oracle to return a version from a different provider than intended, leading to incorrect price feeds being served to markets. The function assumes that at(latestOracleTimestamp) returns a valid version from the correct provider, but at() may return a version from an older provider due to the for-loop logic.

extra_findings.title: Precision Loss in UFixed6 to UFixed18 Conversion in claimFee
extra_findings.description: The claimFee function converts a UFixed6 settlementFeeRequested to UFixed18 using UFixed18Lib.from(settlementFeeRequested). UFixed6 has 6 fractional bits (max precision 1/64), while UFixed18 has 18 fractional bits. When converting from lower to higher precision, the value is left-shifted, but if the original UFixed6 value has non-zero bits beyond the 6th fractional bit (which is impossible by definition), no truncation occurs. However, the reverse is not checked: if the market.claimFee returns a fee that is not representable in UFixed6 (e.g., > 2^6 - 1/64), the subtraction feeReceived.sub(settlementFeeRequested) may underflow or produce incorrect results due to implicit type coercion. The UFixed6 type is used for fee requests, but the actual fee received may exceed its range, leading to silent precision loss.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Not Bound in onlySubOracle Modifier
extra_findings.description: The onlySubOracle modifier authorizes either the current or latest oracle provider to call claimFee. However, the authorization is bound only to the contract address, not to the specific operation context (e.g., settlementFeeRequested). An attacker can front-run a legitimate claimFee call by observing a pending transaction, then submitting their own claimFee with a different settlementFeeRequested value, consuming the authorization nonce and stealing the fee difference. The signature or authorization does not bind the requested fee amount, allowing context manipulation.

extra_findings.title: at() Function Infinite Loop Risk Due to Unbounded For-Loop
extra_findings.description: The at() function iterates from global.current - 1 down to 1 using a for-loop without a bound check on the array size. If global.current is 0 or 1, the loop condition i > 0 may still execute with i = 0, but the real danger is if global.current is very large (e.g., > 2^256 - 1, though unlikely) or if oracles array is sparse. More critically, if global.current is 0, the loop condition i > 0 is false and safe, but if global.current is 1, i becomes 0 and the loop exits. However, if the oracles mapping has gaps (e.g., oracles[5] exists but oracles[4] is uninitialized), the provider assignment may be incorrect. The loop assumes contiguous epochs, but the mapping allows sparse storage. This can cause the function to return a version from an unintended provider, leading to incorrect price feeds.

extra_findings.title: Missing Domain Validation in _latestStale for Timestamp Comparisons
extra_findings.description: The _latestStale function compares timestamps without validating that the timestamps are non-zero or monotonically increasing. If an oracle provider returns a timestamp of 0 (e.g., due to a bug or malicious behavior), the condition 'uint256(oracles[global.latest].timestamp) >= currentOracleLatestVersion.timestamp' may evaluate to true when it should not, causing the oracle to incorrectly believe the latest is not stale. This can prevent oracle updates indefinitely, freezing price feeds. Since timestamps are uint96 and can be 0, and no validation is performed, this creates a denial-of-service vector.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Failure in _updateLatest and _handleLatest Causes Incorrect Oracle Version Retrieval
extra_findings.description: The _updateLatest and _handleLatest functions contain a critical state synchronization flaw where the global.latest pointer is updated based on a stale or inconsistent view of the current oracle's latest version. This causes the at() function to return incorrect or outdated oracle versions when queried, leading to incorrect pricing for derivatives, liquidations, or margin calculations. The issue arises because _handleLatest conditionally re-queries the oracle using at() with a timestamp derived from global.latest, but global.latest may not reflect the true latest committed version due to timing gaps between oracle updates and state commits. This creates a window where users and external systems rely on an outdated price, resulting in financial loss during liquidations or settlements.

extra_findings.title: claimFee Allows Sub-Oracle to Steal Oracle Fees by Manipulating settlementFeeRequested
extra_findings.description: The claimFee function allows a malicious sub-oracle provider to claim more than the actual fee received from the market by setting settlementFeeRequested arbitrarily high. The function calls market.claimFee(address(this)) to retrieve the actual fee, but then sends settlementFeeRequested (controlled by the caller) to msg.sender (the sub-oracle factory), and only returns the difference. Since msg.sender is not validated against the actual oracle provider's address beyond a weak check in onlySubOracle, an attacker can deploy a fake oracle provider that claims to be the current or latest provider, then call claimFee with a large settlementFeeRequested. This results in the market transferring the full fee to the attacker, and the oracle protocol losing the difference between the actual fee and the requested fee. No validation ensures settlementFeeRequested <= feeReceived, enabling theft.

extra_findings.title: request() Function Allows Market to Trigger Unbounded Oracle Updates, Leading to State Bloat and Potential DoS
extra_findings.description: The request() function, callable only by the market, triggers an update to the oracle's current epoch and calls .request() on the underlying provider. However, it does not validate whether the current oracle provider has actually advanced its version since the last request. This allows a malicious market to call request() repeatedly, creating a new epoch entry in the oracles[] mapping for every call, even if no new data is available. Since oracles[] is an unbounded mapping and each entry consumes storage, this leads to exponential state bloat. Eventually, this will cause gas costs for status(), at(), or update() to exceed block limits, rendering the oracle unusable. No rate-limiting, timestamp-based throttling, or version-checking prevents this abuse.

extra_findings.title: at() Function Has Infinite Loop Risk Due to Unbounded For-Loop Over Epochs
extra_findings.description: The at() function iterates backward from global.current - 1 down to 1 using a for-loop without a bound check on the number of epochs. If an attacker has triggered many request() calls (as in the previous vulnerability), global.current can reach very high values (e.g., 10,000+). The loop will then iterate over thousands of entries, consuming more gas than available in a single block. This causes the function to revert on gas exhaustion, making historical price queries impossible. Since at() is used for liquidations, settlements, and dispute resolution, this DoS prevents critical protocol functions from operating, locking user positions and funds indefinitely.

extra_findings.title: onlySubOracle Modifier Allows Any Previously Used Oracle Provider to Claim Fees, Enabling Replay Attacks
extra_findings.description: The onlySubOracle modifier allows either the current or latest oracle provider to call claimFee. However, once an oracle provider is replaced (via update()), it is no longer active but still qualifies as 'latest'. A malicious actor who previously owned an oracle provider can re-deploy the same contract and call claimFee, even if they are no longer the current or latest provider. Since the modifier only checks msg.sender against the stored addresses of current or latest providers, and those addresses are never cleared or invalidated after replacement, this creates a replay vulnerability. An attacker can claim fees indefinitely using old oracle provider addresses, draining the market's incentive pool.

extra_findings.title: update() Function Allows Factory to Bypass Oracle Version Consistency, Leading to Price Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The update() function allows the factory to replace the current oracle provider with a new one, but it does not validate that the new provider's latest() timestamp is greater than or equal to the current provider's timestamp. An attacker controlling the factory can replace the oracle provider with one that reports an older or manipulated price (e.g., a price from 1 hour ago). The _updateCurrent function only checks that global.current == global.latest (to prevent out-of-sync updates), but does not validate temporal consistency of the new provider's data. This allows the factory to roll back the oracle version, causing the system to use an outdated price for pricing derivatives, triggering unjustified liquidations or preventing valid ones.

extra_findings.title: Incorrect Socialization Calculation in _socialize Leads to Permanent Loss of User Assets
extra_findings.description: The _socialize function incorrectly calculates the claim amount by using context.global.assets as the denominator while using context.totalCollateral as the numerator, but context.totalCollateral includes collateral from all markets and is not synchronized with context.global.assets. This causes the socialization multiplier to be greater than 1, allowing users to claim more assets than are actually available in the vault, resulting in permanent loss of protocol assets. The error occurs because context.totalCollateral is the sum of all market collateral (including pending deposits and withdrawals), while context.global.assets represents only the net settled assets. This mismatch causes the formula to overstate the available collateral relative to assets, leading to an inflated claim amount that exceeds the vault's actual asset balance.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Position Reduction via update() Functions
extra_findings.description: The update() functions allow users to reduce their position (e.g., close long/short) or withdraw collateral without requiring users to specify minimum acceptable outcomes. This enables front-running and malicious price manipulation by oracles or MEV bots to force unfavorable position closures, resulting in user losses. There is no slippage tolerance, minimum output, or execution bounds parameter, violating Pattern 1 (User Control Over Execution Outcomes).

extra_findings.title: Validation After State Change in _update() Leading to Invalid Position Updates
extra_findings.description: In _update(), the state is modified (position, pending orders, collateral) before validation via InvariantLib.validate(). This violates Pattern 2 (Validation Timing). If the invariant check fails, the state has already been corrupted, and the revert occurs after irreversible changes. This allows invalid state transitions to be committed temporarily, potentially leading to incorrect accounting or insolvency.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Accounting Between Requested and Actual Execution in _processOrderLocal()
extra_findings.description: In _processOrderLocal(), the function processes a pending order using versioned oracle data (versionTo), but the accounting for fees (liquidationFee, subtractiveFee, solverFee) is based on the original order's metadata, not the actual executed state. If the oracle version is stale or invalid, the order is invalidated (newOrder.invalidate()), but the fee credits to referrers and liquidators still occur using accumulationResponse, which may be derived from invalid data. This creates a mismatch: the position is invalidated (no real exposure change), yet fees are paid out as if the trade executed. This violates Pattern 3: accounting does not align with actual execution outcome. For example: a user places a 100 ETH long order at $2000, but oracle is stale at $1900. Order is invalidated due to stale price, yet $100 in solver fees are still paid to referrer based on accumulationResponse derived from invalid data. User loses no position, but protocol pays out fees incorrectly, draining protocol treasury.

extra_findings.title: Access Control Missing in IMarket Interface for Critical Functions
extra_findings.description: The IMarket interface declares public functions such as update(), settle(), claimFee(), and claimExposure() without any access control modifiers (e.g., onlyOwner, onlyCoordinator). This interface design implies these functions are callable by anyone, which contradicts the actual contract's use of modifiers like onlyOwner, onlyCoordinator, and onlyOperator. This violates Pattern 4: Interface access control expectations. Attackers can exploit this mismatch by calling functions via the interface that should be restricted, potentially bypassing intended access controls if the interface is used by external contracts that assume permissive access.

extra_findings.title: Incorrect Recipient Selection in _credit() for Liquidation Fees
extra_findings.description: In _processOrderLocal(), liquidation fees are credited to liquidators[account][newOrderId], but this mapping is set in _update() only if newOrder.protected() is true (i.e., when msg.sender is the one calling update with protect=true). However, liquidators are also set via external calls (e.g., liquidate() function not shown, but referenced). If a liquidator is set externally and the order is later settled via _processOrderLocal(), the fee is paid to that address. But if the order was invalidated (e.g., stale oracle), the liquidator mapping is not cleared. This creates a scenario where a malicious actor can set themselves as liquidator for a future order ID (via a prior call), then wait for a stale price settlement to trigger a fee payout to themselves — even though no valid liquidation occurred. This violates Pattern 5: Conditional recipient selection does not verify execution validity before payment.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Failure in _settle() Leading to Stale Position Updates
extra_findings.description: In _settle(), the function calls _processOrderGlobal() and _processOrderLocal() to update positions, but the state updates to _position and _positions are only performed in _storeContext(), which is called after _settle() completes. However, during _processOrderGlobal() and _processOrderLocal(), the context.latestPositionGlobal and context.latestPositionLocal are modified in-memory, but if an error occurs during _processOrderLocal() (e.g., oracle revert), the entire transaction reverts — yet the global state (_position) remains unchanged. This is acceptable. However, the issue arises in the 'sync' phase: if context.latestOracleVersion.timestamp > context.latestPositionGlobal.timestamp, _processOrderGlobal() is called with the current latestId (not next). But if the current latestId's order is already processed, this call may process an order that has already been settled, leading to double-counting of position changes. This violates Pattern 6: state is read and modified in a chain where dependent functions may operate on inconsistent state. Example: User has position at timestamp 100. Oracle advances to 105. _settle() calls _processOrderGlobal() with latestId=5 (order at 105). It processes it. Then immediately calls _processOrderGlobal() again with latestId=5 (same order) because context.latestPositionGlobal.timestamp is still 100. This double-applies the order, inflating position and fees.

extra_findings.title: Return Value Unit Mismatch in claimFee()
extra_findings.description: The claimFee() function returns a UFixed6 feeReceived, but internally calls token.push(msg.sender, UFixed18Lib.from(feeReceived)). UFixed6 is scaled by 1e6, while UFixed18 is scaled by 1e18. UFixed18Lib.from(feeReceived) performs a direct bit-cast conversion without scaling: UFixed18Lib.from(x) = UFixed18(x.value). This means a feeReceived of 1e6 (1.0 in UFixed6) becomes 1e6 in UFixed18 (0.000001 in 18-decimal terms), not 1.0. This is a unit mismatch: the function returns a value in 6-decimal units but transfers in 18-decimal units without conversion. This violates Pattern 9 (Return Value Unit Consistency). For example: if a user claims 1000000 UFixed6 (1 token), they receive only 0.001 token. This is a 99.9% loss of claimed fees. The error propagates to all fee claimants, draining protocol revenue.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before External Call in _update()
extra_findings.description: In _update(), state is committed via _storeUpdateContext() before the token transfers (pull/push) occur. If the token.transfer() reverts (e.g., due to insufficient balance or paused token), the state changes (position, pending orders, referrer assignments) are already committed. This violates Pattern 7 (State Commitment Timing). An attacker can call update() with a malicious token contract that reverts on transfer, causing the protocol to permanently record a position change and fee assignment without the collateral being moved. This leads to protocol insolvency: users are credited with positions they didn't collateralize, and referrers are paid fees without collateral backing.

extra_findings.title: External Oracle Assumption Violation in _processOrderGlobal()
extra_findings.description: _processOrderGlobal() assumes that oracle.at(timestamp) always returns a valid OracleVersion and OracleReceipt, and that the oracle will never return a version with timestamp < latestPositionGlobal.timestamp. However, if the oracle contract is forked or upgraded (e.g., to a different version with different semantics), the return structure may change. The code assumes fixed ABI: (OracleVersion memory, OracleReceipt memory). If the external oracle returns a different number of values or struct layout, the call reverts. This violates Pattern 8 (External System Assumptions). Since the oracle is external and upgradable, this creates a permanent DoS risk: if the oracle is upgraded to a non-compatible version, _processOrderGlobal() reverts, freezing all settlement for the market. No user can close positions or claim fees.

extra_findings.title: Partial Execution Risk in _settle() with Multiple Order Processing
extra_findings.description: _settle() processes multiple pending orders in while loops. If one order fails during _processOrderGlobal() or _processOrderLocal() (e.g., due to oracle revert or invariant violation), the entire transaction reverts. However, if the oracle is slow and multiple orders are ready, the protocol cannot settle any of them. This is not a direct fund loss, but it creates systemic risk: users cannot exit positions during volatility, leading to forced liquidations or insolvency. More critically, if an attacker triggers a revert in one order (e.g., by manipulating oracle data for one ID), they can prevent settlement of all pending orders for that account, locking user funds indefinitely. This violates Pattern 9 (Systematic Partial Execution Analysis): the function does not handle partial success, and users have no mechanism to settle individual orders. This is a protocol-level DoS vector.

extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds via External Call Returns
extra_findings.description: The Vault contract has no protection against external calls returning funds to the contract during settlement or rebalance operations. When external markets (via _settleUnderlying()) return collateral to the vault, these funds are indistinguishable from user deposits and are immediately consumed by the _manage() function for rebalancing. This prevents users from successfully withdrawing their funds because withdrawal amounts are treated as new deposits and reallocated to markets, effectively locking user funds in the protocol.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in _update Function - No Minimum Output Bounds for RedeemShares
extra_findings.description: The _update function allows users to redeem shares without any mechanism to specify a minimum acceptable asset output. This enables front-running and MEV attacks where an attacker can manipulate market prices between the user's redemption request and execution, causing the user to receive significantly fewer assets than expected. The function uses UFixed6Lib.MAX as a magic value to redeem all shares, but provides no protection against unfavorable execution outcomes.

extra_findings.title: Validation Timing Vulnerability in _update Function - State Changes Before Validation
extra_findings.description: The _update function performs state changes (context.global.update, context.local.update, context.currentCheckpoint.update) before validating critical invariants like depositAssets.gt(_maxDeposit(context)) and redeemShares being within bounds. This allows invalid operations to partially execute before being reverted, potentially leaving the vault in an inconsistent state or enabling front-running of state updates.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Accounting in _socialize Function - Misuse of context.global.assets in Redemption Calculation
extra_findings.description: The _socialize function incorrectly uses context.global.assets in the socialization formula, which represents the total assets in the vault before the current operation. However, the function is called during _update, where depositAssets and redeemShares are being processed. This causes the socialization calculation to use stale values, leading to incorrect asset distribution. For example, if a user redeems 100 shares worth 1000 assets, but context.global.assets is 5000 (from previous state), the socialization formula will incorrectly calculate the claim amount based on outdated total assets, resulting in users receiving less than their fair share.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Issue in _settle Function - Global State Updated Before Local State
extra_findings.description: The _settle function updates global state (context.global.processGlobal) before settling local state (context.local.processLocal). However, _manage is called after _settle and depends on context.global.assets and context.global.deposit to calculate eligible collateral. If a user redeems shares during the same transaction, the _manage function will use the updated global state before the local state is settled, leading to incorrect collateral allocation calculations. This creates a window where the vault's internal accounting is inconsistent, potentially causing over-allocation of collateral or under-collateralization.

extra_findings.title: Return Value Unit Mismatch in _checkpointAtId Function - Returns PerennialCheckpoint Without Proper Scaling
extra_findings.description: The _checkpointAtId function returns a PerennialCheckpoint struct containing collateral, tradeFee, and settlementFee values that are aggregated from external markets. However, these values are not scaled to match the UFixed6 unit used throughout the vault. When these values are used in _manage and _ineligible functions, they are treated as UFixed6 values, but they are actually in the external market's native unit (likely 18 decimals). This unit mismatch causes incorrect calculations in _ineligible, where context.totalCollateral (UFixed6) is subtracted by context.global.assets (UFixed6) and context.global.deposit (UFixed6), but the aggregated collateral from _checkpointAtId is treated as if it were in the same unit. This leads to massive underestimation of eligible collateral, causing the vault to under-allocate and lock user funds.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Timing Vulnerability in _update Function - State Committed Before External Calls
extra_findings.description: In the _update function, state is committed via _saveContext before the _manage function executes external calls to market.update. If any market.update call fails (e.g., due to insufficient liquidity or reentrancy), the state changes (context.global.update, context.local.update, context.currentCheckpoint.update) have already been committed, consuming the user's deposit/redeem request. This creates a scenario where users pay gas and lose assets without receiving the intended outcome, and the protocol cannot revert the state to its original condition.

extra_findings.title: External System Assumption in _registerMarket - No Validation of Market Oracle Sync
extra_findings.description: The _registerMarket function assumes that all markets are on the same 'clock' (same oracle timestamp) as stated in the contract docstring, but does not validate this assumption. It only checks that the market's token matches the vault's asset. If a malicious actor registers a market with a different oracle update frequency or timestamp drift, the vault's _settleUnderlying function will use inconsistent timestamps, causing incorrect checkpoint calculations and potential asset misallocation. This breaks the core invariant of the protocol and can lead to systemic insolvency.

extra_findings.title: Partial Execution Risk in _manage Function - Market Updates May Partially Fail
extra_findings.description: The _manage function iterates over markets and calls market.update for each. If one market.update call reverts due to insufficient liquidity or other reasons, the entire transaction reverts, but the state changes from _update (context.global.update, context.local.update) have already been committed. This creates a scenario where users have their shares redeemed or assets deposited, but the underlying collateral is not properly rebalanced, leading to permanent misallocation of assets and potential protocol insolvency. There is no mechanism to handle partial success or rollback collateral adjustments.

extra_findings.title: Oracle Factory Allows Reinitialization of Already-Created Oracles via update()
extra_findings.description: The update() function allows an owner to replace the underlying oracle provider for an existing oracle instance without validating that the new provider is compatible with the oracle's current state or that the oracle's internal logic can safely handle the swap. This creates a critical state inconsistency risk: if the new oracle provider has different data structures, fee models, or price aggregation logic, the oracle's output can become corrupted or manipulated, leading to incorrect pricing in dependent DeFi protocols. Since oracles feed prices to collateralized lending, derivatives, and AMMs, this can cause systemic insolvency. The vulnerability is exacerbated by the fact that the oracle's ID remains unchanged, so external systems continue to reference the same oracle address while its underlying logic is replaced with arbitrary, potentially malicious code.

extra_findings.title: create() Function Allows Creation of Oracle with Invalid or Zero Address via factory.oracles(id)
extra_findings.description: The create() function calls factory.oracles(id) to obtain an oracle provider address, but does not validate that the returned address is a deployed contract with expected functionality. An attacker can register a malicious IOracleProviderFactory that returns address(0) or a non-oracle contract (e.g., a simple ERC20) for a given id. The create() function then proceeds to deploy a new oracle instance using _create() with abi.encodeCall(IOracle.initialize, (address(0), name)), which will revert during initialization due to invalid parameters. However, if the malicious factory returns a non-zero but non-oracle address (e.g., a contract without initialize() or with incompatible signature), the _create() call may succeed but produce a non-functional oracle. Subsequent price queries on this oracle will fail silently or return garbage data, corrupting all dependent protocols. No validation ensures the returned address implements IOracleProvider correctly, creating a silent failure vector.

extra_findings.title: updateId() Enables Oracle ID Spoofing and Double-Spending of Oracle Instances
extra_findings.description: The updateId() function allows the owner to arbitrarily reassign any oracle instance to any bytes32 id, bypassing the create() function's uniqueness check. An attacker can create an oracle with id1, then call updateId(oracle, id2) to map the same oracle instance to a second id. Now both id1 and id2 point to the same oracle. If id1 is used in one DeFi protocol and id2 in another, and the oracle's price is updated, both protocols receive the same price — but if one protocol expects a different asset or time window, this causes catastrophic mispricing. Worse, if the oracle is later updated via update(id1, newFactory), the change affects both id1 and id2 simultaneously, creating uncontrolled cross-protocol interference. This breaks the fundamental assumption that each oracle id maps to a unique, independent price feed.

extra_findings.title: withdraw() Function Allows Owner to Drain All Accrued Fees Without Accounting for Oracle-Specific Fee Balances
extra_findings.description: The withdraw() function calls token.push(owner()), which transfers the entire balance of the specified token from the OracleFactory contract to the owner. However, the OracleFactory does not track per-oracle or per-factory fee accruals. If multiple oracles are created and each accumulates fees independently (e.g., via their underlying providers), the total balance in OracleFactory is a sum of all fees. The withdraw() function drains the entire balance without distinguishing which fees belong to which oracle. This allows the owner to steal fees that were intended for oracle providers, liquidity providers, or governance. For example, if Oracle A accrues 1000 USDC and Oracle B accrues 500 USDC, the owner can withdraw 1500 USDC in one call, stealing 500 USDC that should belong to Oracle B's stakeholders. No mechanism exists to distribute or allocate fees correctly.

extra_findings.title: initialize() Function Allows Reinitialization of _parameter After Deployment, Enabling Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The initialize() function calls _parameter.store(OracleParameter(1, UFixed6Lib.ZERO, UFixed6Lib.ZERO)) without checking if it has already been initialized. This means the owner can call initialize() multiple times, resetting the global oracle parameters (e.g., fee rate, slippage tolerance) to zero at any time. If the oracle system relies on these parameters to calculate fees or price adjustments (e.g., a 0.1% fee rate), resetting them to zero allows the owner to disable all fees retroactively. This enables fee avoidance: an attacker could create an oracle, let it accrue fees for days, then call initialize() to reset parameters to zero, and withdraw all fees via withdraw(). The reset invalidates all prior economic assumptions and allows the owner to steal accumulated value. This is a direct economic manipulation vulnerability.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Oracle Creation and Update Allows Unauthorized Oracle Deployment
extra_findings.description: The create() and update() functions are marked with onlyOwner, but the IOracleFactory interface does not declare any access control modifiers. This creates a security mismatch where external systems or auditors relying on the interface may incorrectly assume these functions are publicly callable, potentially leading to unauthorized oracle deployment or manipulation if the interface is used in off-chain logic or by other contracts that assume interface-level access control. Furthermore, the create() function allows any owner to deploy an oracle with any ID and factory, but there is no validation that the oracle provider returned by the factory is authorized or safe, creating a risk of deploying malicious or non-compliant oracle implementations.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Failure in create() Function Allows Oracle ID Hijacking
extra_findings.description: In the create() function, the oracle instance is created via _create() and then assigned to oracles[id] and ids[newOracle] in sequence. However, if the _create() call reverts (e.g., due to internal logic in the oracle implementation), the state variables oracles[id] and ids[newOracle] are still updated, leaving a dangling or invalid oracle entry. This creates a state inconsistency where an oracle ID is permanently reserved but no valid oracle instance exists, preventing future use of that ID. Additionally, if the oracle implementation reverts after the factory.oracles(id) call but before state assignment, the factory's oracle provider may be consumed without proper accounting, allowing an attacker to exhaust valid oracle provider IDs by triggering reverts.

extra_findings.title: No Validation of Oracle Provider Implementation Safety Before Deployment
extra_findings.description: The create() function calls factory.oracles(id) and immediately uses the returned address to deploy an oracle without validating that the returned contract is a legitimate, non-malicious oracle implementation. An attacker can register a malicious IOracleProviderFactory that returns a contract with a malicious initialize() function (e.g., one that transfers funds to the attacker or reverts with a specific pattern). Since the oracle is created via _create(abi.encodeCall(...)), the initialize() function is called immediately with no safeguards. This allows an attacker to deploy a malicious oracle under a legitimate ID, potentially compromising all systems that rely on that oracle's data.

extra_findings.title: Reentrancy Risk in Oracle Initialization via _create()
extra_findings.description: The create() function uses _create(abi.encodeCall(IOracle.initialize, (...))) to deploy and initialize an oracle. The _create() function (inherited from Factory) uses CREATE to deploy a new contract and then immediately calls initialize() on it. If the oracle's initialize() function makes an external call (e.g., to a malicious contract), reentrancy into OracleFactory is possible before the state variables oracles[id] and ids[newOracle] are set. An attacker could exploit this to call create() again with the same ID, bypassing the 'already created' check and deploying multiple oracles under the same ID, leading to oracle ID hijacking and potential data manipulation.

extra_findings.title: Withdraw Function Allows Owner to Drain Any Token Without Restriction
extra_findings.description: The withdraw(Token18 token) function allows the owner to withdraw any ERC20 token held by the contract without any limit or validation. This includes tokens deposited by users for oracle fees, collateral, or other protocol purposes. Since the contract holds no explicit accounting of token balances per token type, the owner can drain any token sent to the contract, including those not intended for withdrawal. This is a critical design flaw: the contract acts as a generic token sink with no safeguards, enabling the owner to steal any deposited assets.

extra_findings.title: Access Control Bypass on _updateMarket Allows Manipulation of Market Weights and Leverage Before Settlement
extra_findings.description: The _updateMarket function is called by public functions updateWeights and updateLeverage, which are restricted to onlyOwner. However, _updateMarket itself is private and not directly callable, but it updates critical state variables (weight and leverage) that are used in the StrategyLib.allocate() calculation during _manage(). The vulnerability arises because _settleUnderlying() is called before updateWeights and updateLeverage, but the actual market weight and leverage changes are not reflected in the global state until the next settlement. An attacker can call updateWeights or updateLeverage immediately before a user calls update() or rebalance(), causing the vault to rebalance based on outdated weights/leverage while the new weights are stored but not yet settled. This allows the attacker to manipulate the allocation of collateral to markets with lower risk or higher yield, effectively stealing value from other users by skewing the portfolio allocation before settlement. The economic impact is a misallocation of collateral that benefits the attacker at the expense of depositors.

extra_findings.title: Unit Mismatch in _socialize Function Causes Incorrect Claim Asset Distribution
extra_findings.description: The _socialize function calculates claimAmount using UFixed6 values but performs a division with context.global.assets (UFixed6) and context.totalCollateral (UFixed6), which are both in the same unit. However, context.totalCollateral is the sum of collateral from all markets, which is tracked as Fixed6 (signed) in the Context struct, while context.global.assets is UFixed6 (unsigned). The function uses UFixed6Lib.unsafeFrom(context.totalCollateral), which interprets a potentially negative Fixed6 value as a large positive UFixed6 due to two's complement wraparound. This causes the min(context.totalCollateral, context.global.assets) to return an incorrect value — often the maximum UFixed6 — leading to claimAssets being multiplied by an inflated factor. As a result, users claiming assets receive vastly more than they are entitled to, while the vault's assets are drained. The call chain is: _update() → _socialize() → miscomputed claimAmount → asset.push() transfers excess assets to user. This is a critical financial loss to the vault.

extra_findings.title: Desynchronized Loop Bounds in _settleUnderlying and _checkpointAtId Cause Incomplete Market Settlement and Checkpoint Aggregation
extra_findings.description: The _settleUnderlying() function iterates over totalMarkets to call settle() on each market. However, totalMarkets is incremented in _registerMarket() without any synchronization with the _registrations mapping. If a market is unregistered (not implemented in code) or if totalMarkets is manually manipulated, the loop may skip markets or access invalid indices. More critically, _checkpointAtId() iterates over context.registrations.length, which is set from totalMarkets in _loadContext(). But if a market is registered after _loadContext() is called (e.g., during a concurrent update), the loop in _checkpointAtId() will not include it, causing the checkpoint to undercount collateral, tradeFee, and settlementFee. This leads to incorrect totalAssets() and totalShares() calculations. For example: if totalMarkets=3, but a new market is registered and totalMarkets=4, then a user calling update() will load context with length=3, and _checkpointAtId() will miss the 4th market's checkpoint. This causes the vault to understate its total assets by the full value of the 4th market's collateral, allowing users to redeem shares for more assets than the vault holds. Mathematical proof: Assume 3 markets each with 1000 assets. totalAssets() = 3000. An attacker registers a 4th market with 1000 assets. totalMarkets=4. A user calls update(). _loadContext() reads totalMarkets=4? No — because _loadContext() is called before the registration completes. If registration happens between _loadContext() and _checkpointAtId(), the loop in _checkpointAtId() still uses length=3. totalAssets() = 3000, but actual collateral = 4000. User redeems 1000 shares (1/3 of totalShares). They receive 1000 assets, but vault actually has 4000 assets and 4000 shares — so they should receive 1000 * (4000/4000) = 1000. But because totalAssets() is reported as 3000, totalShares() is also wrong. If totalShares was 4000, but calculated as 3000, then user redeeming 1000 shares gets 1000 * (3000/3000) = 1000 — which is correct? Wait — no: totalAssets() is computed from checkpoint.assets + deposit - redemption. If checkpoint.assets is undercounted by 1000, then totalAssets() is 2000, totalShares() is 2000. User redeems 1000 shares → gets 1000 * (2000/2000) = 1000. But vault has 4000 assets. So user gets 1000, vault has 3000 left — correct? Not if the user's shares were minted based on the correct 4000 total. The real flaw is that _checkpointAtId() undercounts, so checkpoint.assets is wrong, so totalAssets() is wrong, so convertToAssets() is wrong. A user who deposited 1000 assets when totalAssets=3000 gets 1000 shares. Later, totalAssets becomes 4000 due to new market. User redeems 1000 shares → should get 1333.33 assets. But because checkpoint.assets is still 3000, totalAssets() is 3000, so they get 1000 * (3000/3000) = 1000. Vault loses 333.33 assets. The attacker can register a market with high collateral right before a redemption, then the redemption calculation is based on old checkpoint, stealing value from the vault.

extra_findings.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in _socialize Function: Division by Zero
extra_findings.description: The _socialize function performs a division by context.global.assets without validating that it is non-zero, leading to a silent division-by-zero error that reverts the transaction. However, the function's logic assumes context.global.assets > 0 to proceed with multiplication, but when context.global.assets == 0, the division reverts, breaking the socialization mechanism entirely. This is a domain validation failure: logarithmic/division functions must validate their domain, and here the divisor is unchecked.

extra_findings.title: Incomplete State Restoration in _settle: Global Latest Not Updated for Local Settlement
extra_findings.description: In _settle, when settling a local account (account != address(0)), the function updates context.local.processLocal but does not update context.global.latest even when global checkpoints are processed. This causes a divergence: global.latest may be behind context.global.current, but local settlement uses context.local.current without advancing global.latest. This leads to checkpoint state being inconsistently applied across global and local contexts, causing double-counting or missed socialization in future operations.

extra_findings.title: Precision Loss in UFixed6 Conversion via muldiv: Truncation Without Rounding
extra_findings.description: The convertToShares and convertToAssets functions use muldiv (from Math.sol) which truncates toward zero. When converting between assets and shares, if totalAssets and totalShares are not perfectly aligned (e.g., 1000 assets / 999 shares), a deposit of 1 asset yields 0 shares due to truncation. This causes users to lose fractional share value permanently. For example: totalAssets=1000, totalShares=999, deposit=1 → shares = 1 * 999 / 1000 = 0 (truncated). The user deposits 1 asset but receives 0 shares, and future redemption of 0 shares returns 0 assets — permanent loss.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Binding Failure: update Allows Any Caller to Operate on Any Account
extra_findings.description: The update function allows any caller to operate on any account if they are an operator (via IVaultFactory.operators). However, the authorization (operator status) is not bound to the specific parameters (depositAssets, redeemShares, claimAssets). An attacker can obtain a valid operator signature for a small deposit and then front-run by submitting a malicious update with large redeemShares, draining the victim's position. The signature authorizes 'operator' status but not the operation context — enabling parameter substitution attacks.

extra_findings.title: Interface Incompatibility: _retarget Calls market.update with 5 Params, But Perennial Market Expects 6
extra_findings.description: The _retarget function calls registration.market.update with 5 parameters: (address, position, leverage, collateral, false). However, the Perennial Market interface (as per standard implementation) requires 6 parameters: (address account, uint256 position, uint256 leverage, uint256 collateral, bool isRebalance, uint256 nonce). The missing nonce parameter causes ABI encoding mismatch. The call reverts with 'invalid opcode' or 'call failed' because the function selector matches but the parameter count differs, breaking all rebalancing and causing collateral to be stuck.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Oracle Parameter Updates Enables Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The updateParameter function allows the owner to modify global oracle parameters including fee-related values (feeRate and feeCap), but there is no mechanism to prevent these parameters from being changed after oracles have been created and are actively processing trades. This enables a timing attack where an attacker can manipulate fee parameters to reduce or eliminate fee collection during critical periods, effectively stealing protocol revenue. The parameter values are read during oracle operations (e.g., price updates, fee accruals) but are not snapshotted, allowing the owner to lower fees retroactively or during high-volume periods.

extra_findings.title: Representation Boundary Violation in Oracle Creation: IOracle Interface Mismatch
extra_findings.description: The create function calls _create(abi.encodeCall(IOracle.initialize, (oracleProvider, name))) to deploy a new oracle instance. However, the IOracle interface is not defined in the provided code, and the initialize function signature is assumed to be (IOracleProvider, string). If the actual IOracle implementation expects a different signature (e.g., including fee parameters, timestamps, or additional context), the ABI encoding will be incorrect. This causes the deployment to revert silently or deploy a malformed oracle, breaking the entire oracle lifecycle. Since the oracle's fee calculation logic depends on correct initialization, this leads to uncollectible fees and broken accounting. The representation boundary is violated because the factory assumes a specific initialize signature without verifying compatibility with the actual implementation contract.

extra_findings.title: Data Access Integrity Failure: Oracle ID Mapping Desynchronization Risk
extra_findings.description: The updateId function allows the owner to manually map an oracle instance to an ID, bypassing the create function's validation. However, there is no check to ensure that the oracleProvider passed to updateId was actually created via the factory or that its internal state is consistent with the ID. This creates a desynchronization risk: if an attacker deploys a malicious oracle instance and calls updateId to map it to a valid ID, the system will treat it as a legitimate oracle. Subsequent calls to oracles[id] will return the malicious instance, which could return manipulated prices or refuse to charge fees. This breaks the assumption that all oracles are created through the factory and have consistent initialization. The data structure (mapping of id -> oracle) is accessed by all oracle operations, so this desynchronization corrupts the entire oracle data collection.

extra_findings.title: Incorrect Adiabatic Exposure Calculation Due to Sign Flip Logic Error
extra_findings.description: In _accumulateAdiabaticExposure, the adiabatic exposure is incorrectly split between maker and market by flipping the sign of the total exposure and then conditionally assigning it. The logic assumes that if the maker is zero, the entire exposure should go to the market, but the sign flip causes the market to receive a negative value while the maker receives a positive value — the opposite of economic intent. This results in the protocol incorrectly crediting the maker with positive exposure when it should be debiting it, and vice versa. This leads to permanent misallocation of funding and P&L, causing the protocol to overpay makers and undercharge takers, or vice versa, depending on market direction. The error is mathematically provable and leads to direct loss of protocol revenue or unjust enrichment of users.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Failure in _accumulateAdiabaticExposure Leads to Incorrect Market Exposure Accounting
extra_findings.description: The function _accumulateAdiabaticExposure computes adiabatic exposure based on the difference between oracle prices and current skew, but then incorrectly assigns the entire exposure to the market when maker is zero, while simultaneously reducing the maker's exposure by the same amount. This creates a double-counting error: the market exposure is set to the full value, but the maker exposure is also set to the negative of that value, even when the maker has no position. This causes the market's exposure to be overstated by the full amount, while the maker's exposure is incorrectly reduced. The result is that the market's reported exposure (used in _response to set response.marketExposure) is inflated, leading to incorrect fee calculations and potential misallocation of risk capital. The error occurs because the logic assumes that if there is no maker, the entire exposure should be attributed to the market — but the code then also subtracts that same amount from the maker's value, which is zero, creating a negative balance that is never reconciled. This violates the invariant that total exposure (maker + market) should equal the computed adiabatic exposure.

extra_findings.title: Unprotected State Updates in _accumulateSettlementFee and _accumulateLiquidationFee Enable Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The functions _accumulateSettlementFee and _accumulateLiquidationFee directly modify state variables (next.settlementFee and next.liquidationFee) without access control, allowing any caller to manipulate settlement and liquidation fee accumulation by triggering accumulation with forged OracleReceipt values. Since these fees are used in economic calculations (marketFee, liquidation risk), an attacker can artificially inflate or suppress fees to avoid paying fees or extract protocol revenue. The vulnerability exists because _accumulate is externally callable and does not restrict who can initiate accumulation, enabling front-running or timing attacks where an attacker submits a malicious OracleReceipt to manipulate fee accumulation before legitimate updates.

extra_findings.title: Unit Mismatch in _accumulateAdiabaticExposure Causes Incorrect Market Exposure Calculation
extra_findings.description: The function _accumulateAdiabaticExposure computes adiabatic exposure as (price_delta * exposure), where exposure is derived from skew and scale, but returns it as a Fixed6 value. However, the response struct VersionAccumulationResponse expects marketExposure to be in the same unit as the underlying position scaling (i.e., normalized to the market's position scale). The function does not normalize the exposure by the riskParameter.takerFee.scale before returning it. This causes the marketExposure value in the response to be 1e18 times larger than intended (since Fixed6 uses 1e18 scaling). As a result, downstream systems (e.g., risk engines, liquidation triggers, or external dashboards) that interpret marketExposure as a normalized value will overestimate exposure by 1e18x, leading to incorrect liquidation thresholds and potential under-collateralization. The call chain is: _accumulateAdiabaticExposure → _accumulate → _response → VersionAccumulationResponse.marketExposure. The exposure is used in risk calculations without scaling correction, causing systemic mispricing of risk.

extra_findings.title: Desynchronized Iteration in _accumulateFunding and _accumulateInterest Due to Socialized Position Assumptions
extra_findings.description: The functions _accumulateFunding and _accumulateInterest assume that socialized portions (longSocialized, shortSocialized, socializedMakerPortion) are computed from the full position size and remain consistent across accumulation cycles. However, these values are derived from context.fromPosition, which may have been partially liquidated or adjusted between versions. If a user partially closes a position between oracle updates, the socialized portions are not recalculated to reflect the new position size, but the accumulation still uses the old socialized values. This creates a desynchronization: the funding and interest are distributed based on outdated socialized ratios, leading to overpayment to some parties and underpayment to others. For example, if a long position of 1000 is reduced to 500, but socializedLong remains 1000, then funding intended for 500 is distributed over 1000, effectively diluting the payout by 50%. This results in a permanent loss for the remaining longs and an unfair gain for makers or shorts who receive excess funding. The issue propagates because the socialized values are not updated in the Version struct between accumulations.

extra_findings.title: Incorrect Fee Aggregation in _response Causes Underpayment of Protocol Fees
extra_findings.description: The _response function aggregates marketFee as tradeFee + tradeOffsetMarket + fundingFee + interestFee. However, tradeFee already includes the taker and maker fees from _accumulateFee, and tradeOffsetMarket is a separate component from linear/proportional/adiabatic fees. But in _accumulateFee, tradeFee is computed as makerFee + takerFee - subtractiveFee, while tradeOffsetMarket is computed separately in _accumulateLinearFee and _accumulateProportionalFee. This results in double-counting of taker fees: takerFee is included in tradeFee, and takerPos/takerNeg linear/proportional fees are also included in tradeOffsetMarket. Since tradeOffsetMarket is meant to be the market's share of price impact, not a separate fee, including it in marketFee causes the protocol to collect fees twice for the same economic activity. For example, if takerFee = 100 and tradeOffsetMarket = 50, marketFee becomes 150, but the actual fee generated is only 100. This leads to a 50% overstatement of protocol revenue, which may trigger incorrect incentive distributions or risk modeling. The error is systemic because marketFee is used in governance and reward calculations.

extra_findings.title: Incorrect Fee Distribution in settle() Leads to Unauthorized Fund Transfer
extra_findings.description: The settle() function incorrectly transfers the asyncFee to msg.sender (the caller of settle()) instead of the keeper who provided the price update. This allows any caller to claim the asyncFee reward intended for the oracle keeper by calling settle() on any version, even if they did not provide the price. The asyncFee is computed and stored during commit() based on the gas oracle cost, but is misattributed during settlement. This results in unauthorized fund extraction by malicious actors who call settle() without performing any keeper work.

extra_findings.title: OracleFactory.updateId() Allows Oracle ID Hijacking via Address Reuse
extra_findings.description: The updateId function allows any oracle instance to be mapped to any arbitrary oracle ID, even if that ID was previously used by a different oracle. This enables an attacker to hijack an existing oracle's identity by reassigning its ID to a malicious oracle instance, leading to unauthorized control over oracle data and potential financial manipulation.

extra_findings.title: create() Function Commits State Before External Call Validation
extra_findings.description: The create() function commits the oracle instance to the oracles[id] mapping and updates the ids mapping before verifying that the underlying oracle.initialize() call succeeded. If the external initialize() call reverts (e.g., due to gas limits, invalid parameters, or malicious implementation), the oracle instance is still registered in the mappings, creating a zombie oracle that cannot be used but consumes the ID permanently.

extra_findings.title: update() Function Allows Oracle Factory Replacement Without Validation of New Oracle Instance
extra_findings.description: The update() function allows the underlying oracle provider to be replaced by any registered factory, but does not validate that the new oracleProvider returned by factory.oracles(id) is a valid, initialized, or compatible oracle instance. An attacker can register a malicious factory that returns a non-functional or malicious oracle, causing oracle data to become stale or corrupted without any error.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation in updateParameter() Allows Invalid OracleParameter Values
extra_findings.description: The updateParameter() function accepts any OracleParameter value without validating its components. OracleParameter contains two UFixed6Lib values (likely representing min and max deviation thresholds). If these values are set to zero, negative, or astronomically large values, the oracle may behave unpredictably (e.g., reject all updates, accept all updates, or cause arithmetic underflow/overflow in downstream contracts). No domain validation is performed.

extra_findings.title: OracleParameter Storage Uses Uninitialized UFixed6Lib Values with No Normalization
extra_findings.description: The OracleParameterStorage uses UFixed6Lib.ZERO as default, but the type may allow multiple bit representations for the same semantic value (e.g., different exponent encodings). If the UFixed6Lib type does not normalize values before comparison (e.g., 1.0e0 vs 0.1e1), equality checks in downstream logic may fail silently. No evidence of decode/normalize steps exists in the code, risking inconsistent behavior in threshold comparisons.

extra_findings.title: Desynchronized Iteration in settle() Leads to Missed Settlement Callbacks and Fee Theft
extra_findings.description: The settle() function iterates over _localCallbacks[version] using a fixed maxCount and removes the first element (index 0) in each iteration. However, EnumerableSet.AddressSet.remove() does not preserve order, and removing the first element repeatedly while the set is being modified can cause the iteration to skip elements. This results in some callback addresses never being settled, causing their settlement fees to be permanently lost. The fees intended for those users are instead claimed by the factory (msg.sender) without proper settlement, creating a systematic theft of user fees.

extra_findings.title: Unrestricted Access to _commitRequested Allows Fee Manipulation via Timing Attack
extra_findings.description: The _commitRequested function is only called by commit(), which is restricted to onlyFactory, but the logic inside _commitRequested uses block.timestamp to determine whether a price is timely. However, the timeout check is performed on next() (the next requested version), which is controlled by the oracle provider via request(). An attacker who controls the oracle provider can delay calling request() until just before timeout, then trigger a commit() with an invalid price, forcing the system to use the previous price and still charge a syncFee. This allows the attacker to avoid paying the full syncFee for stale prices by manipulating the timing of request() calls, effectively stealing fees from the protocol.
