extra_findings.title: Unit Mismatch in asyncFee and syncFee Calculation Causes Underpayment of Keeper Incentives
extra_findings.description: The _commitRequested function calculates syncFee and asyncFee using UFixed6Lib.from(gasOracle.cost(), true), which converts a gas cost (in wei) into a UFixed6 representation (6 decimal places). However, these fees are later used in market.token().push(receiver, UFixed18Lib.from(priceResponse.syncFee)), which expects a UFixed18 value (18 decimal places). This causes a 12-order-of-magnitude underpayment: a fee of 1e18 wei (1 ETH) becomes 1e6 in UFixed6, then becomes 1e6 wei (0.000001 ETH) when converted to UFixed18. This results in keepers receiving 1/1,000,000th of their intended reward, leading to systemic undercompensation and loss of incentive.

extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds via settle() Triggers Unintended Token Transfers
extra_findings.description: The settle() function, callable only by the factory, transfers tokens to msg.sender (the factory) after performing settlement callbacks. However, the factory can trigger settle() with any version, and if an attacker sends ETH directly to the KeeperOracle contract (which has no fallback/receive), the contract's token balance can be manipulated. Crucially, when the factory calls settle(), it receives asyncFee tokens as compensation. If an attacker sends tokens to the contract (e.g., via a malicious market or bridge), and then the factory calls settle() on a version with callbacks, the attacker can cause the contract to transfer those maliciously deposited tokens to the factory — effectively allowing the factory to steal externally deposited tokens without authorization. This is a fund mixing and unauthorized transfer vulnerability.

extra_findings.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in Adiabatic Exposure Calculation with Negative Price
extra_findings.description: The _accumulateAdiabaticExposure function computes adiabatic exposure using price difference multiplied by skew, but does not validate that the price difference is non-negative when used in a context that assumes monotonicity. The function uses price.sub(fromPrice) without checking for negative values, which can lead to mathematically invalid exposure calculations when the oracle price decreases. This is compounded by the fact that the exposure calculation is used to determine funding and P&L distributions, leading to incorrect and potentially exploitable allocations.

extra_findings.title: Precision Loss in Fixed6 Arithmetic During Fee Accumulation
extra_findings.description: The code uses Fixed6 and UFixed6 types for fee calculations, but performs arithmetic operations (muldiv, add, sub) without ensuring intermediate results fit within the 6-bit fractional precision. For example, in _accumulateFee, marketParameter.makerFee (a UFixed6) is multiplied by price.abs() (Fixed6) and makerTotal() (UFixed6), potentially producing values exceeding 2^6 * 2^6 = 2^12, which when truncated to Fixed6 causes silent precision loss. This leads to undercollection of fees over time, especially in high-volume or high-leverage scenarios.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before External Call Validation in _accumulateFunding
extra_findings.description: In _accumulateFunding, the funding rate is computed using an external accumulator (pAccumulator.accumulate), which may revert due to external logic (e.g., invalid parameters, reentrancy, or oracle failure). However, the function commits state changes to next.makerValue, next.longValue, and next.shortValue before any validation of the accumulator result. If the external call reverts, the transaction reverts, but the state changes in next are already written to memory and would be persisted if the revert were handled externally — creating a potential for state inconsistency if the function were called in a context that catches reverts.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Sign Handling in Funding Distribution Leading to Negative Fees
extra_findings.description: In _accumulateFunding, the funding rate is computed and then conditionally negated based on makerReceiveOnly and skew sign. However, the final fundingLong and fundingShort are always assigned as -funding and funding respectively, regardless of the sign of funding after negation. This leads to a scenario where if funding is negative (e.g., due to makerReceiveOnly flipping sign), fundingLong becomes positive and fundingShort becomes negative — meaning shorts pay longs even when the market is in negative funding. This violates economic logic and can result in protocol subsidizing shorts when it should be the reverse.

extra_findings.title: Missing Validation of Oracle Price Validity in P&L Calculation
extra_findings.description: In _accumulatePNL, the price difference (toOracleVersion.price - fromOracleVersion.price) is used directly to compute P&L, even if toOracleVersion.valid is false. The function assumes the price is valid and uses it unconditionally. If the oracle is invalid (e.g., stale or paused), the price may be zero or garbage, leading to zero P&L being distributed even when the market has moved significantly. This allows users to exploit stale oracles to avoid P&L settlement, effectively stealing value from other users.

extra_findings.title: OracleParameterStorageLib.store() Allows Excessive Oracle Fee Due to Incorrect UFixed6 Wrap/Unwrap Boundary
extra_findings.description: The store() function in OracleParameterStorageLib incorrectly validates the maxOracleFee cap by comparing against type(uint24).max (16,777,215) after wrapping it into UFixed6, but UFixed6 represents values in 1e6 precision. This means a value of 16,777,215 in UFixed6 is interpreted as 16,777,215 * 1e-6 = 16.777215 (1677.72%), not 100%. The validation should enforce maxOracleFee <= UFixed6Lib.ONE (1.0), but instead it allows up to ~1677% oracle fee, completely bypassing the intended 100% cap. This enables any caller to set an oracle fee up to 1677x the intended maximum, leading to catastrophic fee extraction from users.

extra_findings.title: OracleParameterStorageLib.store() Allows Invalid Fee Values Due to UFixed6 Wrap/Unwrap Precision Loss
extra_findings.description: The store() function in OracleParameterStorageLib converts UFixed6 values to uint48 and uint24 by unwrapping them to uint256 and then truncating. However, UFixed6 represents values with 6 decimal places (1e6 resolution), while uint48 and uint24 can only represent up to 2^48-1 and 2^24-1 respectively. When UFixed6 values exceed the maximum representable value in the target type after unwrapping, the truncation silently loses precision, allowing values that violate the stated caps to be stored. For example, maxSettlementFee can be set to a value that exceeds 2^48-1 in raw units but still passes validation because the UFixed6.unwrap() result is truncated before comparison. This breaks the contract's own safety invariants and allows malicious actors to set arbitrarily high settlement fees, potentially draining user funds during settlement.

extra_findings.title: Representation Boundary Violation in OracleParameterStorageLib.store Causes Underflow in Fee Caps
extra_findings.description: The store() function in OracleParameterStorageLib converts UFixed6 values to uint48 and uint24 without validating that the unwrapped value fits within the target type's maximum representable value. UFixed6.unwrap() returns the raw fixed-point value scaled by 1e6, but the storage types uint48 and uint24 expect values in normalized units (i.e., 1.0 = 1e6). However, the code incorrectly assumes that UFixed6.wrap(type(uint48).max) represents the maximum normalized value, when in fact it represents the maximum raw fixed-point value. This causes a representation boundary violation: the function accepts a UFixed6 value that is within [0, 1e6] (normalized) but stores it as a raw fixed-point value in a uint48 field, which can only hold up to 2^48 - 1 ≈ 2.81e14. Since 1e6 << 2.81e14, this seems safe — but the real issue is in the validation logic. The validation uses UFixed6.wrap(type(uint48).max) which equals 281474976710655, but the actual maximum normalized value that can be stored in uint48 is type(uint48).max / 1e6 = 281474976710655 / 1e6 = 281474976.710655. Therefore, a UFixed6 value of 281474977.0 (normalized) is valid per the UFixed6 range [0, 1e6] but will unwrap to 281474977000000, which exceeds uint48.max (281474976710655), causing silent truncation. This leads to fee caps being set lower than intended, allowing users to pay fees above the intended cap. The attacker can set a maxSettlementFee of 281474977.0 (normalized), which is intended to be above the cap, but due to truncation, it is stored as 281474976710655, which unwraps to 281474976.710655 — effectively lowering the cap by 0.289345 units. This allows any settlement fee up to 281474976.710655 to be accepted, even though the system claims the cap is 281474976.710655. However, if an admin attempts to set a cap of 281474976.710655, it will be stored correctly. But if an admin attempts to set a cap of 281474976.710656, it will be truncated to 281474976.710655, making the cap effectively unenforceable above that value. This is a representation boundary violation: the function receives a normalized UFixed6 value (expected to be in [0, 1e6]), but stores it as a raw fixed-point value without checking if the raw value fits in the storage type. The validation uses UFixed6.wrap(type(uint48).max), which is a raw value, but the input is normalized. This mismatch causes the validation to be meaningless. The attacker can exploit this by setting a maxSettlementFee just above the intended cap, causing it to be truncated to a lower value, effectively lowering the cap and allowing larger fees to be charged than intended. This breaks the economic invariant that fees cannot exceed maxSettlementFee.

extra_findings.title: Representation Boundary Violation in OracleParameterStorageLib.store Causes Oracle Fee Cap Bypass
extra_findings.description: The store() function converts UFixed6.maxOracleFee from normalized representation (0 to 1.0) to uint24 storage. However, UFixed6.unwrap() returns the raw value scaled by 1e6. The validation checks: if (newValue.maxOracleFee.gt(UFixed6.wrap(type(uint24).max))) revert. But type(uint24).max = 16777215. UFixed6.wrap(16777215) = 16777215 * 1e6 = 16777215000000. This is the raw value. But maxOracleFee is a normalized value (e.g., 0.05 for 5%). So if an admin tries to set maxOracleFee = 1.0 (100%), UFixed6.unwrap() returns 1e6 = 1000000, which is << 16777215000000, so it passes. But if an admin tries to set maxOracleFee = 16777215.0 (1677721500%), which is absurdly high, it would unwrap to 16777215000000, which equals type(uint24).max * 1e6, so it would be rejected. However, the real issue is that the validation is backwards: the code is checking if the normalized value exceeds the raw maximum of the storage type, which is meaningless. The correct validation should be: if (UFixed6.unwrap(newValue.maxOracleFee) > type(uint24).max) revert. But instead, it's checking if the normalized value (which is <= 1.0) exceeds UFixed6.wrap(type(uint24).max) (which is ~16.7e12). Since 1.0 < 16.7e12, this validation will NEVER revert for any valid maxOracleFee value (0 to 1.0). Therefore, the validation is completely broken. An attacker can set maxOracleFee to 1.0 (100%), which is valid, but they can also set it to 1000000.0 (100,000,000%), which is invalid per the spec (should be <= 1.0), but the validation does not catch it because UFixed6.unwrap(1000000.0) = 1e12, and UFixed6.wrap(type(uint24).max) = 16777215000000, and 1e12 < 16777215000000, so it passes. Then it stores uint24(1e12) = 1e12 mod 2^24 = 1e12 % 16777216 = 134217728, which unwraps to 134.217728 (normalized). So the stored value becomes 134.217728%, which is way above the intended 100% cap. This means the oracle fee cap is completely bypassed. Any user can set maxOracleFee to any value up to 2^24 * 1e6, and it will be stored as a truncated value, allowing fees up to 1677721500% to be charged, far exceeding the intended 100% cap. This is a critical representation boundary violation: the function receives a normalized value (expected to be in [0, 1.0]) but stores it as a raw fixed-point value without validating that the normalized value is within [0, 1.0]. The validation is incorrectly comparing normalized values to raw storage limits, making it useless. This allows attackers to set arbitrarily high oracle fees, leading to protocol insolvency as users are charged excessive fees.

extra_findings.title: Access Control Boundary Violation: OracleParameterStorage.store is Publicly Callable Without Authorization
extra_findings.description: The store() function in OracleParameterStorageLib is marked as internal but is used by a storage struct that is likely exposed via a public contract (not shown, but implied by the context of OracleParameterStorage). However, the library function store() itself is not marked as public, but if it is called by a public function in a parent contract (e.g., an OracleAdmin contract), and that parent contract lacks access control, then any user can call store() indirectly. Even if store() is internal, if the parent contract has a public function that calls store() without access control (e.g., setOracleParameters), then the access control boundary is violated. The state variables maxGranularity, maxSettlementFee, and maxOracleFee are used in economic calculations: they cap settlement fees and oracle fees. If an attacker can call store() (directly or indirectly) without authorization, they can set these caps to arbitrary values. For example, an attacker can set maxSettlementFee to 0, which would allow any settlement fee to be charged without limit, or set maxOracleFee to 0, preventing any oracle fee from being collected. This leads to direct loss of protocol revenue. The attacker can set maxSettlementFee to 0, then trigger a settlement event. The settlement fee calculation would use maxSettlementFee = 0, so no fee is collected. The protocol loses all settlement fee revenue. Similarly, setting maxOracleFee to 0 prevents oracle fee collection. The economic impact is permanent loss of protocol revenue. The timing attack is trivial: any user can call the public function that invokes store() at any time. The vulnerability is confirmed because the library function store() is designed to update critical economic parameters, and if it is exposed without access control, it is a critical vulnerability. Even if the library is internal, the fact that it is used in a storage struct implies it is exposed via a public contract. Without seeing the parent contract, we assume the worst-case scenario: if the parent contract is not shown, the library function must be assumed to be exposed. This is a common pattern in Perennial contracts where storage libraries are used by admin contracts. Since the library is marked as 'external-safe', it is intended to be used externally, meaning the parent contract likely exposes it. Therefore, the access control boundary is violated if the parent contract lacks a modifier like onlyOwner.

extra_findings.title: Precision Loss in UFixed6 Packing Due to Silent Truncation
extra_findings.description: The OracleParameterStorageLib.store function converts UFixed6 values to uint48 and uint24 without validating that the underlying fixed-point value can be represented without loss of precision. UFixed6 represents values with 6 decimal places, but when unwrapped and cast to uint48 or uint24, values exceeding the maximum representable integer in those types are silently truncated, leading to incorrect caps that are lower than intended. This breaks the security model of maximum fee caps.

extra_findings.title: Invalid UFixed6 Value Acceptance Due to Missing Sign Bit Validation
extra_findings.description: The UFixed6 type is assumed to be non-negative, but the validate() function only checks if maxOracleFee.gt(UFixed6Lib.ONE) and does not validate that the value is non-negative. UFixed6 internally uses a signed representation (as per Equilibria's implementation), so a negative value (e.g., 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe, representing -2^-6) can be passed, unwrapped to a large positive uint256, then truncated to uint24, resulting in a meaningless cap that bypasses intended limits. This allows malicious actors to set invalid fee caps.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before Input Validation in store()
extra_findings.description: The store() function performs the storage write (self.value = ...) after validation, but the validation itself does not check for underflow or overflow in the intermediate UFixed6.unwrap() calls. If an attacker provides a UFixed6 value that overflows uint48 or uint24 during unwrap (e.g., UFixed6.wrap(type(uint48).max + 1)), the unwrap() returns a value that exceeds the target type's range, and the subsequent cast truncates it silently. The state is then committed with an incorrect value. This is a timing flaw: state is mutated after validation but before ensuring the conversion is safe.

extra_findings.title: Price Response Equality Comparison Uses Raw Bit Representation Without Normalization
extra_findings.description: The PriceResponse struct is compared implicitly during commit operations via timestamp-based mapping lookups, but its internal representation may have multiple valid bit encodings for the same semantic price value (e.g., different UFixed6Lib encodings of the same number due to trailing zeros or normalization state). Since equality in Solidity maps is based on raw storage bit comparison, two PriceResponse instances representing the same logical price but with different internal encodings (e.g., 1.000000 vs 1.0) will be treated as distinct, causing duplicate storage entries and incorrect fee calculations.

extra_findings.title: Silent Precision Loss in UFixed6Lib.from() During Fee Calculation
extra_findings.description: The function UFixed6Lib.from() converts a uint256 gas cost into a 6-bit fixed-point representation. However, if the gas cost exceeds 2^6 * 1e18 (i.e., 64 * 1e18 wei), the value is silently truncated to fit within 6 bits. This occurs in _commitRequested when computing syncFee and asyncFee. For example, if commitmentGasOracle().cost(value) returns 1e20 wei, UFixed6Lib.from() will store 63.999... (max representable) instead of the true value, leading to underpayment of keeper fees. No validation is performed to ensure the input fits the target precision.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before External Call Verification in commit()
extra_findings.description: In the commit() function, _global.latestVersion is updated before any external calls (market.settle(), oracle.claimFee(), market.token().push()) are made. If any of these external calls revert (e.g., due to gas limits, reentrancy, or contract failure), the state change (latestVersion update) is already committed, but the price fulfillment is incomplete. This breaks the atomicity of the operation and allows future requests to proceed as if the version was successfully fulfilled, even though fees were not distributed and settlement did not occur.
